findings.title: LiDAR has substantially more distant object support in this subset
findings.statement: At 150–400 m, 2,309 annotated observations have 91.73% LiDAR support and 15.16% radar support. The actual maximum object centre is 229.42 m.
findings.implication: Retain LiDAR as the stronger geometric reference for these labelled distant objects.
findings.limits: At least one in-box return; LiDAR-conditioned labels; recorded radar boundary near 190 m; not detector recall or a universal ranking.

findings.title: LiDAR scan motion changes the apparent benefit of radar
findings.statement: On the same 25,117 observations, individual-point ego-motion correction reduces radar-only support from 185 to 39.
findings.implication: Deskew before attributing complementary detections to a sensor.
findings.limits: Ego correction only; moving targets and cabin motion remain unresolved.

findings.title: The residual radar-only result depends on box boundaries
findings.statement: Expanding every box face by 0.5 m reduces radar-only observations from 39 to 3 over the same 25,117 objects-at-time observations.
findings.implication: Inspect geometry and residual timing before assigning a physical cause to these cases.
findings.limits: Expanded boxes admit background returns and are a sensitivity test, not corrected ground truth.

findings.title: Radar support varies substantially by class even nearby
findings.statement: At 0–25 m, radar supports 99.12% of 339 truck observations, 67.66% of 201 adult-pedestrian observations and 39.00% of 100 cone observations.
findings.implication: Report vulnerable road users and small obstacles separately from large vehicles.
findings.limits: Class, view, distance within the band and occlusion differ; reflectivity is not isolated; repeated observations.

findings.title: Changing car identities alone does not explain the range decline
findings.statement: For the same 237 car tracks, equal-track radar support falls from 79.95% at 0–50 m to 52.46% at 50–100 m. LiDAR changes from 99.81% to 98.55%.
findings.implication: Follow the same tracks across ranges rather than relying only on a changing pooled population.
findings.limits: Viewpoint, occlusion and target motion are still uncontrolled.

findings.title: The distant support difference persists when scenes get equal weight
findings.statement: At 150–400 m, equal weighting of 9 eligible scenes gives a LiDAR-minus-radar difference of 73.11 percentage points; the smallest scene difference is 57.14 points.
findings.implication: The pooled result is not explained solely by one scene having many labels.
findings.limits: Descriptive scene sensitivity; selected mini scenes and radar range truncation remain; no population confidence interval.

findings.title: The few radar-only observations mostly concern cars
findings.statement: Cars account for 33 of 39 exact-box radar-only observations; trailers and trucks contribute two each, and a bicycle and child pedestrian one each.
findings.implication: Prioritise the car cases for overlay and timing inspection when investigating complementarity.
findings.limits: Counts describe annotation observations, not independently recovered objects or successful detections.

findings.title: The pooled long-range vehicle result extends beyond TruckScenes' radar coverage
findings.statement: At 200–400 m, 504 vehicle observations from 55 tracks have 84.72% LiDAR and 35.52% radar support under the acquisition-time hypothesis. Static values are 80.36% and 37.50%.
findings.implication: LiDAR is the stronger source of distant vehicle geometry in this selected TruckDrive cohort.
findings.limits: Four eligible clips from five preselected clips; different sensor platform; alignment hypothesis is not verified publisher deskew; not AP.

findings.title: Radar complements LiDAR despite lower pooled geometric support
findings.statement: The aligned distant cohort contains 25 radar-only observations. Union-of-support rises from LiDAR's 84.72% to 89.68%; 52 observations have neither modality inside the exact box.
findings.implication: Test the radar-only cases with a fusion detector rather than discarding radar on aggregate density.
findings.limits: Annotation-conditioned geometric union, not fusion-detector accuracy or evidence that all added cases are independent objects.

findings.title: A single radar return often does not mean a dense object representation
findings.statement: Requiring three in-box returns at 200–400 m changes radar-supported observations from 179 to 51 of 504. LiDAR retains 81.15% support versus radar's 10.12%.
findings.implication: Assess spatial information and temporal/Doppler use before treating one return as sufficient recognition evidence.
findings.limits: Three returns is a diagnostic threshold, not a detection criterion; modalities carry different information.

findings.title: A small matched passenger-car cohort reverses the pooled ordering
findings.statement: For 7 passenger-car tracks across 3 scenes appearing in both range bands, equal-track far support is 27.86% LiDAR versus 50.00% radar at 200–400 m under the aligned, exact-box assumption.
findings.implication: State the population in every sensor comparison; retain counterexamples.
findings.limits: Small, selected and box-margin-sensitive cohort; does not negate the larger mixed-vehicle result.

findings.title: Timing can dominate the apparent inability to see thin roadwork objects
findings.statement: For the same 170 barrel observations at 100–150 m, LiDAR support is 28.82% with static calibration and 94.71% under the acquisition-time correction hypothesis.
findings.implication: Validate timestamps and overlays before calling an unsupported barrel a physical sensor failure.
findings.limits: Correction is a sensitivity hypothesis; object motion, label dimensions and extrinsics still matter.

findings.title: Removing any one eligible scene retains the distant vehicle advantage
findings.statement: Equal-scene LiDAR-minus-radar support at 200–400 m is 44.09 percentage points under alignment. Removing any one eligible scene leaves at least 37.75 points.
findings.implication: The selected distant-vehicle result is not driven only by the largest scene.
findings.limits: Descriptive robustness within four eligible clips, not statistical generalisation to all roads or weather.

findings.title: Nearby rocks and building surfaces can be misinterpreted as ground
findings.statement: In the 24-frame patch-64 diagnostic, 813/2012 nearby rock points (40.41%) and 11584/91660 building points (12.64%) receive ground predictions.
findings.implication: Include these terrain failure cases before claiming reliable off-road obstacle handling.
findings.limits: Returned LiDAR points and coarse challenge taxonomy; not percentages of whole rocks/buildings missed or driving-safety scores.

findings.title: Distant obstacle-labelled points are more often assigned ground in this subset
findings.statement: Obstacle-candidate points assigned ground rise from 2.99% of 508,645 points at 0–25 m to 14.17% of 10,173 at 100–150 m.
findings.implication: Report obstacle-to-ground confusion by class and range, alongside ground correctness.
findings.limits: Scene/class composition changes; point percentages are not object miss rates and do not isolate range as a cause.

findings.title: One scenario hides much of the distant ground variation
findings.statement: Ground correctness at 100–150 m is 97.67% when points are pooled, but 89.34% with equal scenario weight. One scenario supplies 85.09% of the 4,888 ground points.
findings.implication: Use per-scenario denominators and macro summaries when explaining terrain performance.
findings.limits: Several scenario denominators are tiny; equal weighting is sensitivity, not an unbiased population estimate.

findings.title: Attention context is a confirmed contributor to selected terrain failures
findings.statement: With checkpoint, input frames, seed and preprocessing fixed, patch 64→256 reduces pooled rock-to-ground confusion from 49.52% to 22.56%. Correct rock-category predictions reach only 24.90%.
findings.implication: A compatibility setting can contribute to model errors; compare configurations before blaming the sensor.
findings.limits: Three adjacent post-hoc frames; partial improvement; no general benchmark or recommended full-split memory setting.

findings.title: The nearby rock error is concentrated in one concrete failure case
findings.statement: One frame supplies 788 of 813 nearby rock-to-ground errors (96.92%). Its labelled rock points span three frame-local instances.
findings.implication: Show the actual difficult frame and test comparable independent cases.
findings.limits: Three frame-local instances are not three independent repeated experiments; nearby views are correlated.

findings.title: Correct ground grouping can hide incorrect surface material
findings.statement: In the earlier ten-frame flight subset, only 34/149 asphalt points at 100–150 m receive artificial-ground predictions; 96 are called natural ground.
findings.implication: Keep material recognition distinct from a binary ground/obstacle grouping.
findings.limits: Tiny distant asphalt denominator; different subset from the 24-frame diagnostic; not a 64-class model evaluation.

findings.title: Higher aggregate accuracy at distance can reflect an easier class mixture
findings.statement: Flight-subset point accuracy rises from 83.40% nearby to 96.90% beyond 150 m, where 94.74% of labelled points are vegetation.
findings.implication: A rising aggregate score does not demonstrate that long-range terrain recognition improves.
findings.limits: Single scenario and interrupted model run; class composition, visibility and point selection remain entangled.

findings.title: Simple voxel collisions do not explain the inspected rock/building case
findings.statement: The inspected rock/building points have 0 same-voxel ground/ground-cover collisions across the tested 2.5 cm and 5 cm grids.
findings.implication: Do not attribute this case to simple ground/obstacle voxel merging; attention context remains the tested contributor.
findings.limits: Only this case and these voxel scales; does not exclude all preprocessing effects or label errors.

findings.title: Low rock geometry is associated with ground confusion
findings.statement: With a ground/ground-cover reference within 1 m in XY, 84.52% of 394 rock points within ±0.2 m vertically are called ground, versus 23.46% of 260 at 0.5–1 m.
findings.implication: Include low protruding rocks when designing an off-road follow-up.
findings.limits: Nearest-point height proxy in one case, not validated object height or an isolated causal geometry effect; snow causality unproven.

findings.title: Radar ground support and raised-geometry support are different questions
findings.statement: In the lake recording, aligned radar supports 4.82% of 13,128 near-ground reference voxel observations and 26.30% of 4,741 raised-geometry observations.
findings.implication: Separate ground mapping from the study of protruding obstacles.
findings.limits: LiDAR-derived reference, 0.8 m tolerance and declared ROI; physical radar extrinsics and visibility unresolved; conditional descriptive result.

findings.title: An unresolved coordinate origin can reverse a terrain conclusion
findings.statement: Farmland radar support is 29.53% raised versus 17.76% ground with the bridged origin; the ROS origin gives 19.33% raised versus 24.07% ground.
findings.implication: Obtain independently validated numerical radar-to-LiDAR transforms before ranking terrain performance.
findings.limits: Both conventions are sensitivity assumptions, not a proven calibration or complete uncertainty interval.

findings.title: One recording does not capture the variation in radar ground support
findings.statement: With the aligned convention, pooled ground support is 17.76% in farmland, 4.82% in lake and 0.94% in land, from 20 sampled frames per recording.
findings.implication: Retain environment-specific results rather than reporting one off-road percentage.
findings.limits: Recording names are publisher categories, not confirmed weather/terrain treatments; calibration and reference bias prevent a causal environment claim.

findings.title: Radar can retain visible evidence in LiDAR-empty annotated fog footprints
findings.statement: At 50–75 m, 9/19 vehicle observations pass the >20-level local radar contrast criterion, while 0/19 exact footprints contain above-ground LiDAR returns.
findings.implication: The fog case motivates a matched weather/fusion experiment and prevents a blanket sensor ranking.
findings.limits: Radar-derived labels, four tracks across the pilot, no clear-weather control; signal contrast is not detection accuracy or proof that fog caused LiDAR absence.

findings.title: Brightness alone also passes many unlabelled control regions
findings.statement: The basic radar contrast test passes 32/117 unlabelled controls; the >20-level test passes 8/117. At 50–75 m, the strict test passes 1/57 controls.
findings.implication: Use background controls and threshold sensitivity when presenting a bright radar footprint.
findings.limits: Controls are unlabelled, not verified empty negatives; these fractions are not false-positive rates or independent significance tests.

findings.title: The far LiDAR sparsity persists under an optimistic footprint/timing sensitivity
findings.statement: At 50–75 m, a 1 m footprint expansion gives LiDAR support in 1/19 observations; allowing either adjacent scan as well gives 2/19.
findings.implication: A small footprint expansion alone does not account for all LiDAR-empty far footprints in this pilot.
findings.limits: Future/adjacent scans are an optimistic offline sensitivity, not a real-time sensor score; target/ego motion and occlusion remain unresolved.

findings.title: A close file timestamp does not mean the whole scans were simultaneous
findings.statement: Three newly decoded radar scans span 249.980–249.997 ms each; the nearest LiDAR scans span 103.271–103.760 ms. File offsets range from -44.910 to +16.267 ms.
findings.implication: Deskew rolling scans using individual point/azimuth timestamps when moving scenes are compared.
findings.limits: First three chronological scan pairs from one sequence; no motion-error magnitude, weather effect or object accuracy measured.

findings.title: Recorded range support depends on the radar representation
findings.statement: Each sample radar image has 3360 range bins, with the documented offset giving a last-bin centre of 199.8864 m. Each paired LiDAR scan contains returns beyond 200 m, with observed maxima 231.00–231.76 m.
findings.implication: Do not score this recorded radar image outside its stored range and interpret the absence as failed object recognition.
findings.limits: Radar bins are intensity samples, LiDAR values are spherical ranges; no shared object/visibility denominator or general hardware range ranking.

findings.title: The official 3D validation subset has narrow recording coverage
findings.statement: The pinned official opt3d split contains 7,517 training, 356 validation and 2,705 test frames. All 356 validation entries belong to K-01; training and test each cover five recording groups.
findings.implication: Use the independent terrain test groups and group-specific scores when checking generalisation from GOOSE.
findings.limits: Metadata audit only; no raw labels or inference. Shared recording groups are not proof of leakage, and do not establish geographic independence.

findings.title: Camera and LiDAR split totals are not automatically a paired population
findings.statement: The opt2d test has 2,133 frames and opt3d test 2,705; only 2,061 frame IDs occur in both. No exact train/val/test frame IDs overlap within either dimension.
findings.implication: Join identical frame IDs before any camera-versus-LiDAR terrain comparison.
findings.limits: Identity check alone does not validate timing, projected-label completeness, spatial disjointness or an accuracy comparison.
